The Quiet Persistence of Wonder

There is a particular quality to early morning light that I find myself thinking about often, even though it is something so common that most people pass through it without notice. It happens in that narrow window before the world fully wakes—when the sun has risen but hasn't yet committed to the business of illuminating everything with the flat, honest brightness of midday. In those minutes, shadows are still long and soft, and the light itself seems to carry some kind of hesitation, as if it is still deciding what to reveal and what to keep gentle.

I have come to believe that wonder is a lot like that kind of light. It doesn't announce itself with fanfare. It doesn't demand your attention. It simply arrives, quietly, in the spaces between the obvious things, and if you happen to be looking in the right direction, you catch it. The trick, of course, is that you almost never know in advance which direction is the right one.

I have been thinking lately about how easy it is to lose this capacity. Not all at once, not in some dramatic moment of realization, but slowly, the way a stone is worn smooth by water. School teaches you that there are right answers. Work teaches you that there are efficient processes. The news teaches you that the world is a complicated and often troubling place. And all of these things are true. But somewhere along the way, the texture of daily life can become so familiar that you stop noticing it. The coffee becomes routine. The walk to the train becomes commute. The faces you pass become part of the scenery rather than whole, irreducible human beings with their own inner weather.

And yet.

There are these moments, these small interruptions in the ordinary flow, that refuse to be fully domesticated. A stranger laughs at something on their phone, and the sound of it is so genuine, so unguarded, that you find yourself smiling for reasons you couldn't explain if someone asked. You see a dog waiting patiently outside a shop, its ears pricked forward with the absolute focus of an animal that has decided this is the most important thing in the world, and for a second, you remember what that kind of focus felt like. You bite into a piece of fruit in season, and the flavor is so vivid, so specific to that moment and that place, that you understand suddenly that you are eating sunlight stored in sugar, and that this is somehow a kind of miracle that you have been taking for granted your entire life.

I don't think we need to manufacture wonder. I think the world is constantly offering it. The problem is that we get so good at filtering, at categorizing, at deciding what matters and what doesn't, that we unconsciously screen out exactly the kinds of things that would otherwise stop us in our tracks. We become, as it were, too efficient. We process the world so quickly that we forget to actually experience it.

There is a quote I've carried with me for years, though I can't remember who said it. Something about how the privilege of a lifetime is to become who you truly are. I used to think that meant something grand, some heroic journey of self-discovery. But I think now that it might be much smaller, and much harder, than that. I think it might mean learning to be present in your own life. Learning to notice the light. Learning to stay curious about the people around you, including the ones you've known for years and have somehow decided you already understand. Learning to ask questions you don't know the answers to. Learning, as we say, to keep your heart soft, even when the world is offering you plenty of reasons to harden it.

This is harder than it sounds. There is real pressure, both internal and external, to have things figured out. To have a position on every issue, a plan for every contingency, an explanation for every failure. And I understand that pressure, because I feel it too. But I have started to suspect that the people I admire most, the ones who seem most fully alive, are not the ones with the most answers. They are the ones who have somehow managed to keep asking questions. They are the ones who are still surprised by things. They are the ones who, when you talk to them, make you feel as if the world is a little larger and stranger and more interesting than you had assumed.

I think about my grandmother sometimes, who lived into her nineties and who I have never heard say a mean word about anyone. She was not an educated woman in the formal sense, but she was one of the wisest people I have ever known. She used to sit on her porch in the evenings and watch the light change on the hills behind her house, and she never seemed bored by it. Not once. She would say things like, "Look at that. Would you just look at that." And she meant it. She was genuinely astonished, every single time, by the same basic fact of beauty that the world kept offering her.

I used to think she was being simple. Now I think she was being profound. Now I think she understood something that the rest of us, with all our cleverness and our categories and our opinions, are constantly in danger of forgetting. The world is astonishing. It really is. And the only thing required to see this is the willingness to look.

So that is what I am trying to do, more or less. To look. To stay open. To let the light in, especially when it is coming through some small and ordinary window that I would otherwise walk past without noticing. To keep becoming, in the small and quiet way that is available to all of us, someone who is still capable of being surprised.

It is not a dramatic project. It will not make headlines. But I have come to believe that it is, in its own modest way, the work of a lifetime.
